facts.summary: Hawaii's statewide minimum wage is $16.00 per hour effective January 1, 2026, higher than the federal $7.25; it is scheduled to rise to $18.00 on January 1, 2028.
facts.sourceAgency: Hawaii Department of Labor and Industrial Relations, Wage Standards Division
facts.notes: Rate confirmed via DLIR news release. Next scheduled increase to $18.00 on 1/1/2028. A tip credit is permitted under HRS 387-2 subject to notice conditions.

facts.summary: Hawaii requires overtime at 1.5x after 40 hours in a workweek, mirroring federal FLSA; there is no general daily-overtime requirement (only public-construction work under Chapter 104 requires daily OT).
facts.sourceAgency: Hawaii Department of Labor and Industrial Relations, Wage Standards Division
facts.notes: General private-sector OT tracks the 40-hr/week federal standard. Daily OT (after 8 hrs) applies only to public works under HRS 104-2(c).

value: domestic or sexual violence victim status
facts.summary: Hawaii's employment discrimination law (HRS ch. 378) protects many classes beyond the federal set, including sexual orientation, gender identity/expression, marital and civil-union status, credit history, arrest/court record, and domestic/sexual violence victim status.
facts.notes: List drawn from HRS 378-2 and the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission. Verify exact current enumerated classes against the statute text, as the legislature periodically adds bases.

facts.summary: Hawaii's discrimination law covers employers with one or more employees, far broader than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.notes: HRS 378-1 defines 'employer' as any person having one or more employees (excluding the United States); the legislature intended employers of all sizes to be covered.

facts.summary: Hawaii's Whistleblowers' Protection Act prohibits discharging, threatening, or discriminating against an employee who reports (or is about to report) a suspected violation of law to a government body or the employer.
facts.notes: Remedies (HRS 378-63/378-64) can include reinstatement, back wages, benefits, damages, and attorney's fees; under HRS 378-65 violators are fined not less than $500 nor more than $5,000 per violation.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the Hawaii Civil Rights Commission within 180 days of the alleged discriminatory act (or the last act in an ongoing practice).
facts.notes: HCRC is Hawaii's Fair Employment Practices Agency; the federal EEOC deadline may be longer (up to 300 days) for dual-covered claims.

facts.value: next working day (discharge); next regular payday (quit without notice)
facts.summary: A discharged employee must be paid all wages in full at the time of discharge or by the next working day; an employee who quits without notice is paid by the next regular payday, or at the time of quitting if at least one pay period's notice was given.
facts.sourceAgency: Hawaii Department of Labor and Industrial Relations, Wage Standards Division
facts.notes: HRS 388-2(b) also requires regular wages be paid within 7 days after the end of each pay period. No general state severance-pay mandate exists.

facts.value: 6 years for a private wage lawsuit (general contract/debt limitation); the Dept. of Labor will only accept an assignment of a wage claim for administrative collection within 1 year of when the wages became due
facts.summary: Hawaii's wage-payment law sets no dedicated limitations period for a private lawsuit to recover unpaid wages, so the general 6-year period for actions on a contract or liability applies; separately, the Director of Labor and Industrial Relations may not accept an assigned wage claim for administrative collection more than 1 year after the wages became due.
facts.citation: HRS § 657-1(1) (six-year limitation for actions upon a contract, obligation, or liability); HRS § 388-11(b) (1-year window for the Director to accept an assigned wage claim)
facts.notes: HRS Chapter 388 (Payment of Wages) does not itself specify a limitations period for an employee's private civil action under HRS 388-11(a); the general 6-year 'debt founded upon contract' catchall in HRS 657-1(1) is the period commonly applied. The 1-year figure in HRS 388-11(b) governs only the Director's acceptance of an assigned claim for the state to pursue on the employee's behalf, not a private lawsuit deadline.
